questions.scenario: A customer-support agent has two client tools: `get_customer` (returns profile and contact data) and `get_order_details` (returns order status and line items). Each description is a single line such as "Retrieves customer information." When users ask "Where is my order?", Claude repeatedly calls `get_customer` and finishes without ever calling `get_order_details`.
questions.stem: Which fix is MOST likely to resolve the misrouting with minimal changes?

options.text: Add a system-prompt table mapping common user questions to the correct tool, so selection is driven by the mapping rather than by the descriptions.
Expand each tool's description to state what it returns, when to use it and when not to (naming the sibling tool), expected inputs, and key limits.
Add few-shot examples of correct conversations to the system prompt that show the right tool being selected for order questions.
Replace both tools with a single combined tool that returns the customer profile and all order data in one call.

questions.explanation: Tool descriptions are the primary mechanism Claude uses to select tools — the docs call them "by far the most important factor" in tool performance. Thin one-line descriptions cause exactly this kind of sibling-tool confusion. The fix is to make each description state what the tool does, when to use it and when *not* to (naming the similar tool), parameter formats, outputs, and limits.

whyWrong.A: A prompt-level mapping can mask the symptom, but the model still selects tools from their description text; leaving the descriptions thin keeps selection fragile, and the mapping can drift as questions change.
whyWrong.C: Few-shot examples add token cost on every request and are a secondary fix aimed at format consistency; they teach tool boundaries far less directly than the descriptions themselves.
whyWrong.D: Consolidation is a legitimate lever for overlapping wrappers of a single workflow, but these are two distinct lookups; merging them changes the API surface far more than the "minimal changes" qualifier allows.

questions.mindset: The model chooses tools from description text alone — make the descriptions do the routing.

questions.scenario: A team extracts invoice data through a tool whose `input_schema` requires `invoice_id` (string), `total` (number), `currency` (enum), and a `line_items` array, with strict tool use enabled (`strict: true`). In production, a small share of calls pass schema validation yet contain impossible values — for example, a `total` that does not equal the sum of the submitted `line_items` amounts.
questions.stem: What does this behavior tell the team about strict mode, and what should they add?

options.text: Strict mode is failing intermittently; they should treat it as a bug and keep retrying failed extractions until the output validates.
Strict mode only guarantees schema-valid input when a tool call occurs, so they should move the summation check into the prompt and have the model compute the total correctly.

Strict mode guarantees schema-conforming arguments (types, required fields, valid enums), not business correctness; keep it and add handler-side validation that rejects mismatches and feeds the error back for a bounded retry.
Strict mode only takes effect when `tool_choice` is `"any"`, so they should force the tool call to make validation apply.

questions.explanation: `strict: true` uses grammar-constrained sampling to guarantee that tool arguments conform to the schema — nothing more. Cross-field business rules such as "total must equal the sum of line items" are semantic and outside the schema's guarantee, so they must be enforced in the application, with a bounded validation-retry loop that returns the error to the model.

whyWrong.A: Strict mode is working: the arguments match the schema. The failures are semantic, which this schema does not and cannot encode; unbounded retries of the same call are not a fix.
whyWrong.B: Moving arithmetic into the prompt makes correctness less reliable, not more; deterministic checks belong in code, not in model instructions.
whyWrong.D: `strict` is a property of the tool definition and applies whenever the tool is called, including under `auto`; forcing the call adds nothing semantically.

questions.mindset: Schemas guarantee shape; handlers guarantee business rules.

questions.scenario: A triage assistant must classify every incoming support ticket by calling the `classify_ticket` tool. Product now wants each reply to include a one-sentence justification *before* the classification is recorded. The developer keeps `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "classify_ticket"}`, but every response contains only the tool call — no justification text.
questions.stem: Why does this happen, and what is the BEST fix?

options.text: With forced selection the API prefills the assistant turn, so no natural-language text can precede the tool call; switch to `tool_choice: "auto"` and instruct the model to justify briefly, then call the tool.
The model is deprioritizing the justification; move the requirement into the tool's description so it is honored on every call.
The justification text is being stripped during streaming; disable streaming to recover the missing sentences.
The response is being truncated by the output limit; raise `max_tokens` so there is room for text before the tool call.

questions.explanation: Forced selection (`tool_choice` of `any` or `tool`) prefills the assistant message, so no free-text preamble appears before the `tool_use` block — by design. When you want an explanation *and* a tool call in the same turn, use `auto` with an explicit instruction telling the model what to say before calling.

whyWrong.B: Tool descriptions shape when and how tools are called; the missing text is caused by the prefilled assistant turn under forced selection, not by weak instructions.
whyWrong.C: Streaming does not remove content blocks; the text is never generated under forced tool choice.
whyWrong.D: Truncation would surface as `stop_reason: "max_tokens"`; here nothing is cut off, the preamble is suppressed by `tool_choice` semantics.

questions.mindset: Forced tool choice buys guarantees at the cost of preamble text.

questions.scenario: An agent calls the client tool `charge_card`. The payment provider responds with HTTP 429 and indicates the request can be retried in roughly 60 seconds.
questions.stem: What should the harness return to Claude for this call?

options.text: An empty successful result so the conversation can continue without confusing the model about the payment state.
A `tool_result` with `is_error: true` and a message stating the call was rate-limited and can be retried after 60 seconds.
A `tool_result` with `is_error: true` containing the raw stack trace and provider error code for debugging.
No `tool_result`; raise an exception that terminates the agent loop and surfaces the failure to the user.

questions.explanation: A failed tool call should be returned as a `tool_result` with `is_error: true` and an actionable message: what went wrong, whether it can be retried, and what to do instead (the docs' example is literally "Rate limit exceeded. Retry after 60 seconds."). This lets the model choose a sensible next step instead of guessing.

whyWrong.A: Marking a failure as success invites the model to report the charge went through; disguising failed lookups as empty successes suppresses recovery.
whyWrong.C: Stack traces and opaque internal codes are not actionable for the model; error results should say what to try next, not dump internals.
whyWrong.D: A transient rate limit is recoverable; terminating the loop throws away the model's ability to adapt and abandons the in-flight turn.

questions.mindset: Errors are data: tell the model what failed and what to do next.

questions.scenario: A shipping agent's `lookup_rates` client tool calls a carrier API that intermittently times out; re-issuing the identical call a second later usually succeeds. Today every timeout is returned to the model as `is_error`, and the agent wastes turns apologizing and re-invoking the tool itself.
questions.stem: What is the BEST way to handle these transient failures?

options.text: Add a system-prompt rule telling the agent to call the tool again whenever it sees a timeout error.
Increase `max_turns` so the model's retry loop can always run to completion without hitting the turn cap.
Return an empty rate list without `is_error` so the model proceeds using default published estimates.
Retry with backoff inside the tool handler for transient errors, and only return an error to the model when retries are exhausted or it must choose a different path.

questions.explanation: Routine transient retries are deterministic work that belongs in code: the handler should retry with bounded backoff and only escalate an error to the model when a decision is genuinely needed (choose another route, ask the user, give up). This saves turns, tokens, and latency compared to prompt-driven retry.

whyWrong.A: Prompt rules are probabilistic and still burn a full model turn per retry; identical-call retries are exactly what code should absorb.
whyWrong.B: A higher turn cap accommodates the symptom without fixing it — every retry still costs a round trip, tokens, and latency.
whyWrong.C: Proceeding with fallback estimates can be legitimate degradation, but only if the failure is surfaced; an unmarked empty list suppresses the error state and invites confident answers built on stale data.

questions.mindset: Retry what is deterministic in code; escalate to the model only what needs judgment.

questions.scenario: In one assistant turn, Claude emits three `tool_use` blocks: `get_customer`, `get_order_details`, and `issue_refund`. The harness executes the calls, but `get_order_details` fails (the order is locked for editing) and `issue_refund` depends on its output, so the team's code deliberately skips the refund. Their current implementation sends back only the customer result.
questions.stem: What must the harness do to keep the conversation valid and informative?

options.text: Return exactly one `tool_result` per `tool_use`, all together in the next single user message with results before any text — the failed lookup as an error, and the skipped refund as `is_error: true` with a note that it was not executed and why.
Return the successful result now, and send the remaining results in separate follow-up user messages as each becomes available.
Return the successful result plus a text note explaining the refund was skipped, omitting its `tool_result` block entirely.
Execute `issue_refund` anyway so that every `tool_use` has a matching result, then report the outcome to the model.

questions.explanation: Every `tool_use` block must be answered with one `tool_result`, matched by `tool_use_id`, all in the next single user message, with results before any text. If you deliberately skip a call after an earlier failure, you still return a `tool_result` with `is_error: true` saying it was not executed and why (the docs' "Not executed: ..." pattern) — this keeps the protocol valid and tells the model the true state.

whyWrong.B: Splitting results across multiple user messages breaks the expectation that results immediately follow the `tool_use` blocks, and it degrades the model's future parallel tool behavior.
whyWrong.C: A text note is not a `tool_result`; unanswered `tool_use` ids make the next request fail with a 400 about missing `tool_result` blocks.
whyWrong.D: Executing a dependent write action whose input never arrived defeats the purpose of the skip logic; validity is restored by an `is_error` result, not by running the call.

questions.mindset: One tool_result per tool_use, in one message, results first — even for calls you skip.

questions.scenario: An agent uses a server-side tool chain (web search followed by fetches). Mid-task, a response arrives with HTTP 200 and `stop_reason: "pause_turn"`, with no client `tool_use` blocks for the harness to execute.

options.text: Synthesize an empty `tool_result` block for the last server tool and send it back so the server-side loop can resume.
Treat the response as truncation and retry the original request with a higher `max_tokens`.
Send the assistant message back to the API unchanged, keeping the same tools, and let the server-side loop continue.
Convert the remaining research steps into client-side tools and re-issue the original request against them.

questions.explanation: `pause_turn` means the server-tool sampling loop hit its iteration limit. The defined continuation is to send the assistant response back **as-is** — never answered with `tool_result` blocks — with the same tools, and the loop picks up where it paused. It is an HTTP 200 outcome, not an error.

whyWrong.A: Answering `pause_turn` with `tool_result` blocks is explicitly wrong; the assistant content itself must be returned unchanged.
whyWrong.B: `pause_turn` is not truncation (that is `max_tokens`); raising the output limit does nothing for a paused server-side loop.
whyWrong.D: Redesigning the tool chain is unnecessary; the protocol provides a defined, zero-cost way to continue.

questions.mindset: Server tools pause, they don't hand off — resend the assistant turn unchanged.

questions.scenario: A developer defines an internal `query_warehouse` tool. To make it "flexible", they add optional string parameters `api_endpoint`, `auth_token`, and `timeout_ms` to the `input_schema` so Claude can fill them per call. Security review objects: the token must not leak and the endpoint must never be overridden by the model.
questions.stem: Which change BEST addresses the reviewers' concerns?

options.text: Keep the parameters but document safe defaults in their descriptions so the model usually leaves them unchanged.
Enable `strict: true` on the tool so the token format and endpoint URL are validated before each call is made.
Move the current token into the tool's description so it is available on every call without a parameter.
Remove infrastructure parameters from the schema; keep credentials, endpoints, and timeouts in harness configuration, exposing only task-level inputs to the model.

questions.explanation: Credentials, endpoints, and timeouts belong in harness configuration — never in the model-facing schema. The schema should expose only the task-level inputs the model genuinely decides (product, warehouse, quantity). Model-supplied endpoints and tokens are an injection and misuse vector, and tool arguments travel through the conversation history and logs where secrets do not belong.

whyWrong.A: "Usually" is not a control: an optional parameter can still be set by the model or by injected instructions, and the secret leaks whenever it is passed.
whyWrong.B: `strict` guarantees schema-conforming arguments, not secrecy or legitimacy of values; a well-formed leaked token is still a leaked token.
whyWrong.C: The description is model-visible context included in every request and log — an even worse place for a secret.

questions.mindset: The schema carries decisions; the harness carries infrastructure and secrets.

questions.scenario: A support agent can call `process_refund` against a payments backend. Policy: refunds up to $500 may execute automatically; anything above $500 requires human approval before execution; refunds to fraud-flagged accounts must never be issued. The team must guarantee the policy holds on every call.
questions.stem: Where should the refund rules be enforced?

options.text: In the system prompt, with explicit policy statements and few-shot examples of each case so the model applies them reliably.
In code: a programmatic gate (harness check or PreToolUse hook) that inspects the tool input, blocks or defers out-of-policy calls, and routes them to human approval.
In the tool's `input_schema`, by constraining the amount parameter so out-of-policy refunds cannot be submitted.
In a second reviewer model that re-reads each refund request and vetoes it when the request violates policy.

questions.explanation: Must-always and must-never rules need deterministic enforcement. Prompt instructions — however well written — are probabilistic, so thresholds, human-confirmation gates, and fraud blocks belong in programmatic checks that inspect the tool input before execution and route out-of-policy calls to a human. This is the classic pattern of enforcing business limits with a gate rather than wording.

whyWrong.A: Prompts are probabilistic; the stem requires a guarantee, and even excellent prompt policy plus examples can miss on any given turn.
whyWrong.C: Schemas express shape and enums, not dynamic policy: numeric constraints are not enforced by strict mode, and the rule depends on backend state (fraud flags) and on routing to a human — neither expressible in a schema.
whyWrong.D: A second model is still probabilistic and adds latency and cost; it can advise, but it cannot guarantee enforcement.

questions.mindset: Guarantees live in code, not in prompts.

questions.scenario: A team wrapped an internal project-management REST API one endpoint per tool — 18 tools such as `list_users`, `list_events`, `create_event`, `update_event`, and `delete_event`. Since the count grew, the agent picks the wrong tool more often and conversations run long. They want the most effective restructuring.
questions.stem: Which approach BEST follows tool-set construction guidance?

options.text: Keep all 18 tools but rewrite every description to be maximally detailed so the model can distinguish them.
Keep the tools but set `tool_choice: "any"` each turn so the model always commits to one of them quickly.
Consolidate related operations into a few workflow-oriented tools (for example, a single scheduling tool with an action parameter), with namespaced names and high-signal, paginated results.
Split the tools across a second helper agent and have the main agent relay requests to it.

questions.explanation: Guidance is a few thoughtful tools targeting high-impact workflows rather than 1:1 endpoint wrappers — the canonical example is replacing list_users + list_events + create_event with one `schedule_event`-style tool. Selection reliability drops as tool count grows (large sets measurably degrade choice), so consolidation, namespacing, and token-efficient (paginated, high-signal) returns are the proportionate fix.

whyWrong.A: Better descriptions help individual tools, but the size of the set is the problem here — 18 overlapping tools still degrade selection and bloat context.
whyWrong.B: Forcing a tool call changes *whether* a call happens, not *which* tool is right, and it suppresses clarifying text; it is the wrong lever for selection accuracy.
whyWrong.D: Adding an agent hop increases latency and loses fidelity relaying context, without fixing the underlying tool design.

questions.mindset: Design tools around workflows, not endpoints; fewer, better tools select more reliably.

questions.scenario: In the Claude Agent SDK, a developer configures `allowed_tools=["Read", "Grep", "Glob"]`, intending to restrict the agent to read-only tools. During the run the agent requests `Edit`; the normal permission prompt appears, the operator approves it, and a file is modified.
questions.stem: Why did this happen, and what is the correct way to prevent it?

options.text: `allowed_tools` is an auto-approve list, not a restriction — unlisted tools still exist and fall through to the normal permission checks; to remove a capability entirely, set `disallowed_tools` (a bare tool name removes the tool definition) or gate it with permission rules, modes, or hooks.
`allowed_tools` restricts tools only in `default` permission mode; the session ran in `acceptEdits`, which lifts the restriction — rerun in `default` mode.
The `Edit` call happened inside a subagent that ignores the parent's `allowed_tools`; disable subagents to restore the restriction.
`allowed_tools` matches exact names only and `Edit` slipped through a wildcard expansion of the list, so the allow list silently approved it.

questions.explanation: In the Agent SDK, `allowed_tools` **auto-approves** the listed tools; it does not restrict the agent to them. Tools not on the list still exist and simply go through the normal permission flow — which is exactly what the scenario shows: `Edit` prompted, was approved, and ran. To actually remove a capability, use `disallowed_tools` (a bare tool name removes the tool definition entirely), permission modes, a `can_use_tool` callback, or PreToolUse hooks.

whyWrong.B: Permission mode changes how approvals happen, but `allowed_tools` never acts as a restriction in any mode — even in `default`, an unlisted tool simply prompts and can still be approved.
whyWrong.C: Subagents run in the parent's permission mode rather than ignoring it, and nothing in the scenario places the call in a subagent; the premise misdiagnoses the semantics.
whyWrong.D: There is no wildcard mechanism silently approving unlisted tools; `Edit` was never in the list, so nothing in the list approved it at all.

questions.mindset: Allow lists approve; deny lists and hooks restrict.

questions.scenario: A booking agent's client tools wrap several backend services. The team is standardizing error reporting around a taxonomy of transient, validation, business-rule, and permission errors, and wants every failed `tool_result` to give Claude what it needs to choose its next move.
questions.stem: Which TWO pieces of information should every error result include? Choose TWO.

options.text: The full stack trace from the failing service so the model can perform root-cause analysis.
Whether the failure is retryable, and if so, roughly when to retry (for example, "rate limited — retry after 60 seconds").
The model's own confidence score that its original tool arguments were correct.
The error category (transient, validation, business rule, permission) in a machine-readable field.
The complete original request payload so the model can re-derive the correct arguments itself.

questions.explanation: An actionable error result tells the model what to do next. Retryability (with timing) plus a machine-readable category map directly onto recovery paths: transient → wait and retry, validation → fix the arguments, permission or business rule → take a different path or escalate. This is the `errorCategory` + `isRetryable` + human-readable message pattern.

whyWrong.A: Stack traces and internal codes are debugging artifacts, not actionable guidance; the docs call for messages that say what to try instead, not opaque output.
whyWrong.C: Self-reported model confidence is not a property of the error and is poorly calibrated; it adds noise, not a recovery signal.
whyWrong.E: The arguments are already in the conversation history; resending the payload wastes context and can echo sensitive data.

questions.mindset: Structure errors so each category implies a recovery path.

questions.scenario: A research assistant has grown to 25 tools spanning web access, file operations, and internal-data lookups. Context usage is bloated, and the model increasingly selects a rarely used tool when a common one would fit the request.
questions.stem: Which TWO practices directly address this problem? Choose TWO.

options.text: Write longer, fully detailed descriptions for all 25 tools so every tool is completely explained on every turn.
Set `tool_choice: "any"` for open-ended user questions so a tool is always selected without hesitation.
Scope the tool set to what the assistant's role actually needs, removing tools outside its job.
Merge the web tools into one generic `search` tool with no namespace prefix to reduce the count.
Defer rarely used tools so their schemas are not loaded into context until they are needed (for example via tool search or `defer_loading`).

questions.explanation: Two levers fix an oversized tool set: scope tools to the agent's role (out-of-role tools get misused and add noise), and defer rarely used tools so their definitions stay out of context until needed. Both reduce context bloat and measurably improve selection accuracy — large tool sets are a known cause of misrouting.

whyWrong.A: 25 longer descriptions make context bloat worse, not better; description quality is a per-tool lever, not a fix for set size.
whyWrong.B: Forcing a tool call changes whether a call happens, not which tool is chosen, and prevents legitimate no-tool answers.
whyWrong.D: Generic, un-namespaced names increase confusion between similar tools; guidance is distinct purposes per tool with namespacing, not vaguer names.

questions.mindset: Curate the tool set: fewer in context means better choices.

questions.scenario: A document-research pipeline uses the server-side web search tool plus a custom client tool `query_internal_docs`. The new maintainer is unsure which behaviors belong to the harness and which are handled elsewhere.
questions.stem: Which TWO statements correctly describe how these tools behave? Choose TWO.

options.text: For `query_internal_docs`, the harness sees `stop_reason: "tool_use"`, executes the lookup itself, and returns a `tool_result` before the loop continues.
Server tool calls must also be answered with client-generated `tool_result` blocks, otherwise the next request fails with a 400.
Client tool failures are retried automatically by the API, so the handler can safely return an empty success on error.
Server tools run on Anthropic's side; if that loop pauses with `stop_reason: "pause_turn"`, the harness continues by sending the assistant message back unchanged.
Client tools are inherently more reliable than server tools because they bypass the model's tool selection entirely.

questions.explanation: Client tools are executed by your code: `stop_reason: "tool_use"` hands you the calls, and you return `tool_result` blocks. Server tools (such as web search) are executed by Anthropic's infrastructure — you never fabricate results for them; if their internal loop pauses (`pause_turn`), you continue by resending the assistant content unchanged.

whyWrong.B: You do not generate `tool_result` blocks for server tools; they execute server-side, and `pause_turn` is continued by returning the assistant message as-is.
whyWrong.C: Client tool execution is entirely the harness's responsibility; nothing auto-retries your handler, and returning empty success disguises failure.
whyWrong.E: Both tool kinds are selected by the model from context; execution location affects where code runs, not whether selection happens.

questions.mindset: Know who executes the tool: you for client tools, Anthropic for server tools.

questions.scenario: A team is adding Jira and Asana access to a planning agent by wrapping each service's REST API with custom tools. Both services expose search, item retrieval, and comment endpoints with similarly named concepts.
questions.stem: Which TWO practices follow tool-writing guidance? Choose TWO.

options.text: Namespace tool names per service (for example `jira_search_issues`, `asana_search_tasks`) so similar tools remain distinguishable.
Return raw UUIDs for all referenced records because they are compact and unambiguous.
Expose one shared `search` tool for both services and let the model infer the target service from the query text.
Include every field the APIs can return so the model can decide what matters in each case.
Return only high-signal fields with human-meaningful identifiers, and support pagination or range limits to keep results small.

questions.explanation: The tool-writing guidance names both practices explicitly: namespace tool names by service so parallel tools stay distinct, and return only high-signal information — semantic identifiers over UUIDs — with token-efficiency mechanisms like pagination, range selection, and filtering so results stay small.

whyWrong.B: Semantic identifiers (keys, slugs, titles) outperform opaque UUIDs for model comprehension and downstream reasoning.
whyWrong.C: A single ambiguous tool forces the model to guess intent; each tool should have a distinct purpose with an unambiguous name.
whyWrong.D: Returning everything bloats context on every call; curate the response to what is decision-relevant, with sensible defaults.

questions.mindset: Names distinguish parallel tools; payloads respect the context budget.
